cards.title: Why Georgia’s Everyday Greeting Wishes You Victory
cards.body: When you greet someone in Georgia, you do not just say hello—you wish them triumph. The standard Georgian greeting is გამარჯობა (gamarjoba), pronounced "gah-mahr-JOH-bah". Derived from the Georgian word for victory (*gamarjveba*), it reflects a history marked by fighting off invading empires. In response, locals reply with გაგიმარჯოს (gagimarjos), wishing victory back to you.

cards.title: Asking "Are You at Peace?" in Korean
cards.body: To say hello in Korean, you ask about someone's peace. The most common polite greeting is 안녕하세요 (annyeonghaseyo), pronounced "ahn-nyung-hah-say-yo". Built from the word *annyeong*, meaning peace or well-being, the phrase literally asks "Are you in peace?" or "Is your peace secure?" It offers a gentle, respectful warm-up before any conversation begins across South Korea.

cards.title: How Printing Press Noise Gave Us the Word "Cliché"
cards.body: Long before "cliché" described an overused phrase, it was an audio sound in 19th-century printing shops. French printers created metal plates for frequently used text blocks to avoid setting type letter by letter. As molten metal struck the matrix mold, it made a distinctive clicking sound. Printers called this cast plate a *cliché*, mimicking the noise—a term that eventually migrated from printing equipment to repetitive ideas.

cards.title: Why "Quarantine" Literally Means Forty Days
cards.body: The word "quarantine" originated during the 14th-century Black Death as a maritime isolation protocol. To protect coastal cities from plague, Venice made incoming ships anchor offshore before crew and cargo could land. The mandated waiting period lasted forty days, called *quarantena* in Venetian Italian, derived from *quaranta*, the number forty. Though isolation periods vary today, the word still preserves its medieval numerical root.

cards.title: The More Than 1,700 Words Coined by William Shakespeare
cards.body: English speakers owe thousands of everyday terms to William Shakespeare. Language historians estimate that the playwright coined or recorded over 1,700 words by combining existing roots, turning nouns into verbs, and adopting foreign phrases. Words like *lonely*, *bandit*, *dwindle*, *elbow* (as a verb), and *uncomfortable* first appeared in his plays and sonnets, shaping the modern English lexicon forever.
